title: High-Performance Model Serving
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# High-Performance Model Serving

##### The same GPU, 23× the throughput

A team in Pune deployed a 7B model behind FastAPI. The endpoint loaded the model, called `model.generate()` per request, and returned the text. Under load testing with 50 concurrent users it managed **4.2 requests per second** with a p95 latency of 41 seconds. GPU utilisation hovered at 22%.

They swapped the serving layer for vLLM. Same model, same A100, same prompts. Result: **97 requests per second**, p95 of 3.8 seconds, GPU utilisation at 91%.

Nothing about the model changed. What changed was memory management and batching. Naive serving wastes GPU in three specific ways — idle time between requests, fragmented KV cache, and the head-of-line blocking of static batching — and the modern inference servers exist to fix exactly those three things.

##### Why naive serving is so bad

Three compounding problems.

**No batching.** GPUs are throughput machines. Processing one request at a time means the weight read from HBM — which dominates decode cost — is amortised across a single sequence instead of thirty-two. The GPU is mostly waiting.

**KV cache fragmentation.** Traditional implementations pre-allocate a contiguous cache block for each sequence's *maximum* possible length. A request that might generate 2,048 tokens but stops at 60 wastes 97% of its allocation. Measured internal fragmentation in pre-vLLM systems ran 60–80%.

**Head-of-line blocking with static batching.** Batch eight requests together and the batch is not free until the *longest* generation completes. Seven sequences that finish at 40 tokens sit idle while the eighth grinds to 900. Their GPU slots produce nothing.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph Static["Static batching - wasted slots"]
        S1[Req A: 40 tok - DONE, slot idle]
        S2[Req B: 55 tok - DONE, slot idle]
        S3[Req C: 900 tok - still running]
        S4[New request D: WAITING for the whole batch]
    end
    subgraph Cont["Continuous batching - slots refilled"]
        C1[Req A finishes -> D enters immediately]
        C2[Req B finishes -> E enters immediately]
        C3[Req C continues uninterrupted]
    end
```

##### Continuous batching

Continuous (or in-flight) batching operates at the **iteration** level rather than the request level. After every single decode step, the scheduler evicts finished sequences and admits waiting ones. The batch is a living set, not a fixed group.

The effect is large: reported throughput improvements of 5–20× over static batching under realistic mixed-length workloads, because no GPU slot ever sits idle waiting for a straggler. Time-to-first-token also improves dramatically, since a new request does not queue behind an entire batch.

The scheduler has to make a judgement each step: admit a new request (raising throughput, slightly slowing everyone) or continue with the current set (protecting latency). `max_num_seqs` and `max_num_batched_tokens` are how you express that preference.

##### PagedAttention and vLLM

Kwon et al. observed that KV cache fragmentation is the same problem operating systems solved with virtual memory — so they applied the same solution.

Instead of one contiguous allocation per sequence, the cache is divided into fixed-size **blocks** (typically 16 tokens). A per-sequence **block table** maps logical positions to physical blocks, which need not be adjacent. Blocks are allocated on demand as generation proceeds.

Three consequences:

- **Near-zero fragmentation.** Waste drops to under 4%, versus 60–80%. More sequences fit in the same memory, which directly raises batch size and therefore throughput.
- **Copy-on-write sharing.** Parallel samples from one prompt, or many requests sharing an 800-token system prompt, share physical blocks until they diverge. This is what makes prefix caching cheap.
- **Preemption.** Under memory pressure the scheduler can swap a sequence's blocks to CPU or recompute them, rather than OOM-ing.

```python
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

llm = LLM(
    model="mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3",
    quantization="awq",                  # 4-bit — more room for KV cache
    dtype="auto",
    gpu_memory_utilization=0.92,         # fraction of VRAM for weights + cache
    max_model_len=8192,
    enable_prefix_caching=True,          # huge win for shared system prompts
    tensor_parallel_size=1,
    max_num_seqs=256,                    # concurrency ceiling
    max_num_batched_tokens=8192,         # prefill chunk size
    enable_chunked_prefill=True,         # stops long prefills stalling decode
)

params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, max_tokens=512,
                        stop=["</answer>"])
outputs = llm.generate(prompts, params)
```

Serve it with an OpenAI-compatible API:

```bash
python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
  --model mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 \
  --quantization awq --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \
  --max-model-len 8192 --enable-prefix-caching \
  --enable-chunked-prefill --max-num-seqs 256 \
  --enable-lora --lora-modules legal=./adapters/legal support=./adapters/support
```

Two settings deserve attention. **`enable_chunked_prefill`** splits a long prompt's prefill into chunks interleaved with ongoing decode steps — without it, one 8,000-token prompt stalls every other user's token stream for hundreds of milliseconds. **`--enable-lora`** with multiple adapters lets one base model serve many fine-tuned variants, swapping adapters per request; that is how a small team serves fifty customer-specific models on one GPU.

##### The server landscape

| Server | Best for | Batching | Multi-model | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **vLLM** | LLMs on GPU | Continuous + paged | LoRA adapters | Default choice for LLMs |
| **TensorRT-LLM** | Max NVIDIA perf | In-flight | Via Triton | Fastest, but compilation is painful |
| **SGLang** | Structured / agentic LLM | RadixAttention | Yes | Excellent prefix reuse |
| **Triton** | Mixed model zoo | Dynamic | Yes, ensembles | Multi-framework, multi-backend |
| **TorchServe** | PyTorch models | Dynamic | Yes | Simple, PyTorch-native |
| **ONNX Runtime** | CPU / edge / small models | Manual | Via server | Broadest hardware support |
| **Ray Serve** | Composed pipelines | Configurable | Yes | Good for multi-stage graphs |

**Triton** is the right answer when you serve a heterogeneous zoo — a PyTorch embedder, an ONNX reranker, a TensorRT classifier, an ensemble tying them together — behind one endpoint with one metrics story.

```
model_repository/
├── reranker/
│   ├── config.pbtxt
│   └── 1/model.onnx
└── pipeline/
    └── config.pbtxt      # ensemble: tokenize -> embed -> rerank
```

```protobuf
name: "reranker"
platform: "onnxruntime_onnx"
max_batch_size: 64
dynamic_batching {
  preferred_batch_size: [ 16, 32, 64 ]
  max_queue_delay_microseconds: 5000     # wait up to 5ms to fill a batch
}
instance_group [ { count: 2, kind: KIND_GPU } ]
```

`max_queue_delay_microseconds` is the explicit latency-for-throughput dial: waiting 5 ms to assemble a fuller batch is nearly always worth it when p95 budget is hundreds of milliseconds.

**ONNX Runtime** remains the pragmatic choice for embedding models, rerankers and classifiers — export once, run on CPU, GPU, or ARM, typically 2–5× faster than eager PyTorch on CPU:

```python
torch.onnx.export(model, sample, "model.onnx", opset_version=17,
                  input_names=["input_ids", "attention_mask"],
                  dynamic_axes={"input_ids": {0: "batch", 1: "seq"}})

import onnxruntime as ort
sess = ort.InferenceSession("model.onnx",
                            providers=["CUDAExecutionProvider", "CPUExecutionProvider"])
```

##### Latency vs throughput

These are in direct tension, and you must decide which you are optimising before you tune anything.

| Metric | Definition | Matters for |
|---|---|---|
| **TTFT** | Time to first token | Perceived responsiveness in chat |
| **TPOT / ITL** | Time per output token | Streaming smoothness |
| **E2E latency** | TTFT + TPOT × output length | Batch and API consumers |
| **Throughput** | Tokens/sec or requests/sec across all users | Cost per million tokens |
| **Goodput** | Requests/sec meeting the SLA | The honest business metric |

Goodput is the one to optimise. Throughput at a p95 of 40 seconds is worthless if your SLA is 5 seconds.

The knobs, and their direction:

- `max_num_seqs` ↑ → throughput ↑, per-request latency ↑
- `gpu_memory_utilization` ↑ → more KV cache, larger batches, higher OOM risk
- `max_num_batched_tokens` ↑ → better prefill efficiency, longer decode stalls
- Chunked prefill on → smoother TPOT, marginally lower peak throughput
- Quantisation → less weight memory, more KV cache room, higher throughput
- Tensor parallelism → lower latency for a large model, worse per-GPU efficiency
- Prefix caching → dramatically lower TTFT when prompts share a prefix

##### Load testing properly

```python
import asyncio, time, numpy as np, httpx

async def one(client, prompt, results):
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); ttft = None; tokens = 0
    async with client.stream("POST", "/v1/completions", json={
        "model": MODEL, "prompt": prompt, "max_tokens": 256, "stream": True,
    }, timeout=120) as r:
        async for line in r.aiter_lines():
            if line.startswith("data:") and "[DONE]" not in line:
                if ttft is None:
                    ttft = time.perf_counter() - t0
                tokens += 1
    total = time.perf_counter() - t0
    results.append({"ttft": ttft, "e2e": total,
                    "tpot": (total - ttft) / max(tokens - 1, 1), "tokens": tokens})

async def load_test(concurrency: int, n: int, prompts: list[str]):
    results, sem = [], asyncio.Semaphore(concurrency)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(base_url=BASE) as client:
        async def bounded(p):
            async with sem:
                await one(client, p, results)
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        await asyncio.gather(*(bounded(prompts[i % len(prompts)]) for i in range(n)))
        wall = time.perf_counter() - t0
    return {
        "concurrency": concurrency,
        "rps": n / wall,
        "output_tok_per_s": sum(r["tokens"] for r in results) / wall,
        "ttft_p50": np.percentile([r["ttft"] for r in results], 50),
        "ttft_p95": np.percentile([r["ttft"] for r in results], 95),
        "e2e_p95": np.percentile([r["e2e"] for r in results], 95),
    }
```

Three rules for honest numbers. Use **realistic prompt and output length distributions** — a benchmark with uniform 100-token prompts hides exactly the head-of-line problems continuous batching solves. **Sweep concurrency** (1, 4, 16, 64, 256) and plot throughput against p95 latency; the knee of that curve is your operating point. And warm up before measuring, since the first requests pay CUDA graph capture and cache warming.

Production monitoring should track the same metrics plus KV cache utilisation, queue depth, preemption count and GPU utilisation. Rising queue depth with GPU under 80% means you are latency-bound, not compute-bound — usually a batching configuration problem.

##### Common mistakes

- FastAPI plus `model.generate()` in production.
- Static batching with mixed output lengths.
- `gpu_memory_utilization` at 0.99, OOM-ing on the first long prompt.
- No chunked prefill, so one long prompt stalls every stream.
- Prefix caching disabled despite an identical 800-token system prompt on every request.
- Benchmarking at batch 1 and extrapolating to production concurrency.
- Uniform-length synthetic prompts in the load test.
- Tensor parallelism on a model that fits on one GPU, paying communication for nothing.
- Reporting mean latency instead of p95, and throughput instead of goodput.
- No autoscaling signal, so a traffic spike queues indefinitely.

##### Hands-on

Deploy a model twice — once behind a naive FastAPI endpoint calling `generate()`, once with vLLM — and load-test both at concurrency 1, 8, 32 and 128 with a realistic prompt-length distribution. Produce a table of RPS, output tokens/sec, TTFT p50/p95 and E2E p95 for each, and plot throughput against p95 latency. Then toggle `enable_prefix_caching` and `enable_chunked_prefill` individually and quantify each one's contribution.

For the mini-project, stand up a production inference service with vLLM or Triton: dynamic or continuous batching tuned to a stated SLA, a quantised model, prefix caching, health and readiness probes, Prometheus metrics for TTFT, TPOT, queue depth and KV utilisation, and an autoscaling policy driven by queue depth. Load-test it to find the knee of the throughput-latency curve and publish a tuning report that names your operating point, your goodput at that point, and your cost per million tokens. Then write your continuous-batching explanation — the iteration-level scheduler, why static batching wastes slots, and how PagedAttention's block allocation makes larger batches possible in the first place.

##### Key takeaways

- Naive serving wastes GPU three ways: no batching, fragmented KV cache, and head-of-line blocking.
- Continuous batching schedules per iteration, refilling slots the instant a sequence finishes — 5–20× throughput on mixed workloads.
- PagedAttention borrows OS virtual memory: block tables cut fragmentation below 4% and enable prefix sharing.
- Pick the server for the job: vLLM for LLMs, Triton for a mixed zoo, ONNX Runtime for CPU and edge.
- Optimise goodput, not throughput, and find your operating point by sweeping concurrency against p95 latency.

mini_project_reference: Set up a production inference service (vLLM or Triton) with dynamic batching, load-test it, and produce a latency/throughput tuning report.
